html:
The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta reached Delhi in 1334 and stayed about eight years in the service of Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq of the Delhi Sultanate.

He had left his home city of Tangier in 1325 on the pilgrimage to Mecca, and kept going: Egypt, Syria, Arabia, Persia, East Africa, Anatolia and the steppe of the Golden Horde, before crossing the Hindu Kush into India.

The sultan welcomed learned foreigners and made him a qadi, a judge, with a large salary. Ibn Battuta describes the sultan as both lavish and terrifyingly cruel, and he lived in fear after falling from favour. In 1342 he was sent as envoy to China. His party was shipwrecked off Calicut, and he went on alone through the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

Back in Morocco he dictated his travels as the Rihla, a key source for the 14th century Islamic world from Delhi to Mali, which he also visited, as in Ibn Battuta visits Mali.
sum: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta reached Delhi in 1334 and stayed about eight years in the service of Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq of the Delhi Sultanate.
